Total: 16 AP triples.

## Step 2: Find all partitions of {1,...,9} into 3 disjoint AP triples

Each AP triple has sum 3×(middle element), so the three middle elements sum to 15. Fixing the triple containing 1 (which is in {1,2,3}, {1,3,5}, {1,4,7}, or {1,5,9}) and completing:

- **P5** = {{1,5,9}, {2,3,4}, {6,7,8}}

Exhaustive check confirms these are the only 5 partitions.

## Step 3: Key structural observation

Any valid grid determines a **row-partition** P (the three row-sets) and a **column-partition** Q (the three column-sets), both among the 5 partitions above. For the grid to be consistent, every row-triple must intersect every column-triple in **exactly one** element (each cell is the unique element at that intersection).

Conversely, given a valid (P, Q) pair with all intersections of size 1, choosing which triple of P goes to each row (3! ways) and which triple of Q goes to each column (3! ways) uniquely determines a valid grid. So the count per valid pair is 3! × 3! = 36.

The 8 valid ordered pairs all involve P4 = {{1,4,7},{2,5,8},{3,6,9}}.

## Step 5: Compute the total

Number of valid grids = 8 valid (P,Q) pairs × 36 arrangements per pair = **288**.

**Verification of no overcounting:** Each grid uniquely determines its row-sets (hence P), column-sets (hence Q), and which triple is in which row/column (the assignment). So each grid is counted exactly once.

**Verification of completeness:** Any valid grid has rows forming one of the 5 partitions and columns forming one of the 5 partitions. All 25 pairs have been checked.
